I reread these previous posts to my Las Vegas Storyline Tournament
Report, and it got me to thinking. Just how many tournament VTES
games have some of you people played anyway? I currently have 85
tournament games under my belt (4 of which Todd has not processed yet
(OrcCon)), but most of the "Top 20" Players have less than 50. (Kudos
to Robert Goudie and Rob Treasure for not only being #2 and #1
(respectively), but also for having played in so many tournaments.)
And, if I count all my "friendlies" as well, I have played nearly 550
games of Jyhad/VTES. (I know this because I'm so anal I've kept a
tally since I started playing my favorite game on Sept. 29, 1994!)

So, when I look at Martin Cubberly's "17th" place ranking (which it
should be since ties are silly; "Top 20" Players my arse: there are
more than 20 players there!), I also notice Martin has played 28
tournament games. Not bad, I think, not bad, but nothing in
comparison to what Rob Treasure or Robert Goudie have done. And
certainly 28 tournament games doesn't even come close to 85 tournament
games. (While I'm at it, this is for the record: I have been in the
"Top 50" a few times, I placed 5th in the 1999 VTES "World
Championship" (with my Gangrel Bleed Deck, remember, David Tatu?), and
I won two tournaments outright (one constructed and one draft) and
took a 4th place in a third constructed tournament, all at Origins
2000. I guess I have my *moments*!)

Yes, my "ranking" is quite low now--and it'll be even lower after Todd
processes OrcCon--but rankings can and do fluctuate quite wildly.
Ratings (one's scaled score with the 3000 baseline) and game count are
what *really* matter. (Heck, you need 10 tournament games just to get
a rating, which will then also give you a "ranking".) I have to say,
though, that I like to "torpedo" people's ratings/rankings, which is
easy to do with my "sub"par rating/ranking.

One final comment: When, oh when, will we start getting ratings for
limited VTES? I know Ben Peal is a HUGE fan of limited, as I am, but
let's face it, folks, people *are* getting much more serious about
this game, and like it or not, it is becoming more and more like my
other favorite game, Magic. Embrace, yon Methuselahs, there is no
turning back! The NAC and EC have already turned VTES into a serious
competition. Single card prices are looking much more like Magic card
prices these days. Special promo cards. New sets on a relatively
frequent basis. Our game has evolved folks; it's no longer the
"friendly" game of VTES at the tournament. It's for REAL! So, let's
get on with getting limited ratings for people and creating composite
ratings as well (constructed/limited weighted average).

Keith M. Thompson
Prince of Las Vegas

There are two reasons for that, Brian.

First, draft is cheaper. You can play 5 drafts for the same
investment as 3 sealed decks.

Second, straight draft is somewhat less skill-intensive than sealed
deck, meaning that weaker players can often compete with stronger
players, which makes for better games all around. I know that seems
counter-intuitive, but I firmly believe it to be true - and I was
ranked in the top 100 Magic players in the world in limited formats
for more than 2 years, before I all but gave up the game. Rochester
draft is the format used for most high level draft events these days.

> Deckbuilding skills don't do a lot for you with "sealed" decks. In a draft, you use
> your deckbuilding skills to select the cards you need over the cards you need less.
>

Actually, my experience (in Magic) is that you pray you haven't
started drafting the wrong things (that is, the things being drafted
by the guys who are sending packs to you). In Jyhad, this is perhaps
slightly less likely...but I'm willing to bet that if three people are
fighting over Brujah, and one guy is scooping up all the obfuscate
cards at the table, the one guy is going to sweep. The resultant
imbalance in decks is unlikely to occur in sealed.

> Nobody can build a great deck out of a starter and 2 boosters with no ability to
> select anything. Personally, I prefer limited drafts, where each player gets a
> starter or a few boosters (actually, these days, you could get a preconstructed
> starter, I guess), and then draft from a pool of about 3 boosters per player.

I have a feeling that a preconstructed starter would be too much of a
good thing.

If you're going to have a starter and five boosters per player, why
not just play an all-out sealed deck with the product? Or,
alternately, have the judge seperate out the vampires, shuffle them
up, place twice as many vampires on the table face up as you have
players drafting, and Rochester draft the vampires - that way, at
least, you would be able to assess what each of your neighbours is
likely to be drafting, and will be able to put together some coherent
strategy. The draft for the remaining cards in the packs would be
normal - it's WAY too slow to completely Rochester 7 packs.

Messages.Author: Chris Berger
Messages.Body:
"LSJ" <vte...@white-wolf.com> wrote in message
news:3C8CFA79...@white-wolf.com...

> Chris Berger wrote:
> > 1) Because true sealed-deck is silly, because you don't even get a chance to
> > use deckbuilding skills. It simply tests luck and play skill.
>
> ? Only if you require players to use every single card they find in
> their product.
>

Not really. If I have 60-80 random cards to make a deck from, I basically choose the
40 which I can actually use and get rid of the rest. Your hypothetical format where
each player gets a box of starters and a box of boosters would surely allow you to
use deck-building skills, but it's unrealistic. I admit there are *some*
deck-building skills involved in sealed format, and the degree to which they are
involved increases as the card pool increases, but a lot of the more subtle
manifestations of deck-building are lost, as there's a pretty clear line between "I
can use this card" and "I cannot use this card".

A draft format gives you a choice between a lot more cards, except that you must
prioritize which cards are more important for your deck. The main problem is that
drafting an entire deck takes a huge amount of time. Also, if two players are
drafting the same types of cards, they will compete with each other until one
relents, weakening both players.

>
> I'm not following your terminology here, sorry.
>
> The V:EKN rules classify all draft events as "limited" events.
>
> Your description of "limited draft" sound more like, but exactly like, the
> V:EKN Restricted Trade sealed format. [VEKN 7.4]
>
> Is there something I'm missing?
>

Possibly. Restricted Trade format, IIRC, involves players choosing a certain number
of cards from their allotted number of cards to trade to others. So it's certainly
not exactly the same. The idea is to give each player a base of about 40-60 cards.
Then a pool of cards containing 20-40 cards per player is drafted in exactly the same
manner that a normal draft is run. This accomplishes two things:

1) It doesn't take as long as drafting ~80 cards per player (note these numbers are
for library cards... the corresponding numbers for vampires would be something like
6-8 to start with and 6-8 drafted, or more likely simply determined by pack
distribution (2-4 vampires per booster)). In theory, it should take approximately
half as long, however it may be actually shorter because players will know from the
get-go what type of cards they are in need of, because they have a base deck to build
off of.

2) Players are slightly less likely to compete for disciplines. Instead of everyone
at the table trying to get obfuscate/dominate/auspex, and no one bothering with
thaumaturgy/celerity/vicissitude (or whatever disciplines), which can often happen in
a draft, players will already have a set of disciplines that they can reasonably use,
and would be better served to build on those. Not that it will eliminate competition
for cards. People will still want the good masters, and people will likely still
have a few disciplines in common, but random chance should allow for a slightly
smoother distribution of cards.

This style would presumably end up with tuned decks somewhere between Restricted
Trade format (somewhat untuned, as you usually only select your worst cards to trade
away) and standard draft (usually pretty tuned, assuming you weren't competing for
cards too fiercely at your table).

Indeed. Sealed deck involves more choices than draft does, at least
in Magic. In draft, I look at a pack, and I choose the 'best' card.
Then I look at the next pack; if there is a good card of the same
color, I choose that; if there is not, I choose a card of a different
color.

Generally speaking, that's about the last real choice I make. From
then on, I draft the best card available to me in the two colors I
picked from first. Sometimes you have to change colors, because there
are just no cards coming to you, but I've sailed through drafts where
I felt that I made maybe six decisions, none of them hard - and at the
end, I may have spent a little time cutting my deck down to size, but
I always knew 18 or so of the 23 cards I end up playing.

The first choice is blind - I have no idea what the guy who is passing
most of the cards to me is drafting. The second choice is not quite
blind - I know he took a card that he considered better than anything
else in the pack; and if he's an experienced drafter he _probably_
took a card that is in another color from the best card remaining in
the pack. But whether my deck turns out to be amazing, which will
happen if the right packs get opened and my neighbours are drafting
different stuff from me, average, or turns out to be disappointing,
which will happen if my neighbours make similar initial choices to me,
is actually not very much under my control.

Neither is sealed deck, you say? True - but in sealed deck, there
will not be nearly as many AMAZING decks as you'll find in draft, and
the games tend to be slower. Slower games result in more decisions;
and better players fare better as the number of decisions goes up and
up. As a result, it's my firm belief that sealed deck magic is a
better test of skill than booster draft is.

for sealed, or around 100 for booster draft.

total crap for trade will most likely come back at you.

My experience with this is that with the amount of cards you are talking about,
you cannot create decks based around clans, you have to have decks based around
disciplines. That's fine, don't get me wrong, but it will cause some people to
not play, hence you should IMHO use more cards as a base of cards to draw from.

> > Your hypothetical format where
> > each player gets a box of starters and a box of boosters would surely allow
you to
> > use deck-building skills, but it's unrealistic.
>
> Likewise 60-80 is unrealistic (60 is probably low even for draft).
> A realistic number would be 120-160.

In the Sabbat War booster draft I ran last year at Origins, we used 10 packs
(of 11 cards each) per person, and it was *just* enough. I playtested this
format a fair amount before I asked for the product from White Wolf (as they
had to send me *9* boxes for the tournament), so I would petition for 100 cards
minimum if anyone from WW asked me for my opinion.
